latin.213: CAPUT IV. Rursus quaedam observata & reprehensa in eodem Cap. II. Notavi quaedam, Reverende & dilectissime in Christo Frater, in secundo Capite Tui tractatus. Patere me etiam quaedam refellere. Dicis enim quaedam de spiraculo vitae, de ligno vitae, deque morte interminata Adamo, quae, nec probo, nec quid momenti ad id conferant, quod tu eo capite probare instituisti, satis assequor, refutata autem meam causam juvare possunt.
latin.214: Rem ab ovo ut aiunt exorsus observas, Deum inspirasse homini spiraculum triplicis vitae, animalis, quae est corporis per unionem animae illud vivificantis, spiritualis, quae est animae per unionem Spiritus sancti illam sanctificantis, & beatae, quae est animae & corporis per unionem cum Deo utrumque beatum reddentis. Idque hoc uno argumento probas, quia textus hebraeus habet in plurali Numero חַיִּים vitas. Quod mihi videtur debilissimum: passim enim usurpatur plurale illud pro singulari, pro ea una vita, quam tu animalem vocas: obvia sunt exempla: vide Gen. 3. 14. & 23. 1. & 25. 7. 17. & 27. 45. Ps. 17. 14. & 31. 11. Eccles. 2. 17. & 9. 9. Et passim alibi. Immo pro ea imperfecta, qualis est brutorum ut Gen. 7. 15. 22. quibus locis etiam brutis animantibus tribuitur נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים spiraculum, ut tu loqueris, vitarum, nec tamen, opinor, alia vita quam animalis, & quidem destituta ratione.
latin.215: Itaque interpretes omnes quos viderim, vitam verterunt non vitas, & vel nihil mysterii in plurali חַיִּים quaesierunt, vel putarunt eo innui eas vitas, quae ad hominis essentiam & naturam sunt absolute necessariae, vegetativam, sensitivam, & rationalem, quae Zanchii & Parei opinio est non contemnenda: quam enim formatio Corporis, tam haec quoque נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים inspiratio ad hominis fabricationem & compositionem, ac constitutionem pertinebat, ad quam etiam sanctitatem & beatitudinem, introductione Adami, postquam creatus fuit, in paradisum, auctam, libenter refero. Habebat enim se sanctitas ad animam, ut sanitas ad corpus.
latin.216: Itaque quemadmodum in corpore non erat duplex vita, quarum altera posita esset in sanitate, sic non arbitror sanctitatem animae augere numerum vitarum, quibus praeditus fuit Adamus. Magnum enim discrimen observo inter Adami & nostram in Christo sanctitatem. Illa naturalis fuit simul cum natura humana & creata, &, nisi amissa fuisset, propaganda secundum leges naturae, ac propterea mutabilis: haec vero pendet ex dono supernaturali Spiritus Sancti a Christo capite in nos eius membra delapso, quo regeneramur, vivificamur, & veluti animamur ac regimur. Sanctitas Adami conditio erat eius vitae Adami, quam animalem appellas, sine qua creari non potuit a Deo justissimo sanctissimoque, & qua fiebat ut Adamus esset bene comparatus ad objecta naturalia. Nostra tota pendet a revelatione supernaturali, tota tendit in objectum supernaturale, nosque supra conditionem illam naturalem & animalem & mutabilem Adami longe evehit. Itaque natura divina a Petro appellatur, & imago gloriae Christi a Paulo. Sed haec obiter: nihil enim faciunt ad rem quam agimus.
latin.217: Eodem nixus plurali חַיִּים vis arborem vitae certam spem fecisse Adamo harum vitarum continuandarum. Atqui non potuit certam spem fecisse continuandae sanctitatis, in qua vitam spiritualem ponis. Hanc enim continuationem Deus ab Adamo exigebat, non ipsi promittebat: qui si eam promisisset, fecisset procul dubio Adamum impeccabilem: fuisset enim promissio ridicula, efficiam ut perseveres in sanctitate & justitia, modo ne pecces.
latin.218: Huic triplici vitae triplicem opponis privationem seu mortem denunciatam a Deo Adamo ut poenam verbis, morte morieris, asserisque hominem, prout Deus minatus fuerat, mortuum esse. Ego vero (pace tua & aliorum, qui sic tecum sentiunt,) non possum verba illa morte morieris ad mortem spiritualem seu privationem justitiae & sanctitatis transferre. Audi, si placet, rationes meas, & expende: nam, nisi me fallit animus, non sunt de nihilo. Prima ratio. Comminatio opponitur tacite promissioni, poena praemio, mors denunciata vitae promissae. Atqui vita tacite promissa Adamo non erat justitia seu sanctitas, nisi velis promissionis conditionem cum re promissa confundere. Ergo mors denunciata non erat privatio justitiae.

pass_a.213: CHAPTER IV. Again certain things observed and reprehended in the same Cap. II. I noted certain things, Reverend and most beloved Brother in Christ, in the second Chapter of Your treatise. Suffer me also to refute certain things. For you say certain things concerning the breath of life, concerning the tree of life, and concerning the death threatened to Adam, which I neither approve, nor do I sufficiently grasp what moment they contribute to that which you undertook to prove in that chapter; but once refuted they can help my cause.
pass_a.214: Beginning the matter from the egg, as they say, you observe that God breathed into man the breath of a triple life—animal, which is of the body through the union of the soul vivifying it; spiritual, which is of the soul through the union of the Holy Spirit sanctifying it; and blessed, which is of soul and body through union with God rendering both blessed. And this you prove by this one argument, because the Hebrew text has in the plural Number חַיִּים lives. Which seems to me most weak: for that plural is everywhere used for the singular, for that one life which you call animal: the examples are ready to hand: see Gen. 3:14 & 23:1 & 25:7, 17 & 27:45; Ps. 17:14 & 31:11; Eccles. 2:17 & 9:9; and elsewhere everywhere. Indeed for that imperfect life such as belongs to brutes, as Gen. 7:15, 22, in which places even to brute animals is attributed נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים the breath, as you speak, of lives, and yet, I think, no life other than the animal, and indeed destitute of reason.
pass_a.215: And so all the interpreters I have seen rendered life, not lives, and either sought no mystery in the plural חַיִּים, or thought there were hinted by it those lives which are absolutely necessary to man's essence and nature—vegetative, sensitive, and rational—which opinion of Zanchius and Pareus is not to be despised: for as the formation of the Body, so also this inspiration of נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים pertained to man's fabrication and composition and constitution, to which I gladly also refer sanctity and blessedness, increased by Adam's introduction into paradise after he was created. For sanctity stood to the soul as health to the body.
pass_a.216: And so just as in the body there was not a double life, of which one would be placed in health, so I do not think the sanctity of the soul increases the number of lives with which Adam was endowed. For I observe a great difference between Adam's sanctity and ours in Christ. That was natural, created together with human nature, and, unless it had been lost, to be propagated according to the laws of nature, and therefore mutable: but this depends on the supernatural gift of the Holy Spirit fallen from Christ the head into us his members, by which we are regenerated, vivified, and as it were animated and ruled. Adam's sanctity was a condition of that life of Adam which you call animal, without which he could not have been created by the most just and most holy God, and by which it came about that Adam was well fitted to natural objects. Ours depends wholly on supernatural revelation, tends wholly to a supernatural object, and carries us far above that natural and animal and mutable condition of Adam. And so it is called divine nature by Peter, and the image of the glory of Christ by Paul. But these things by the way: for they do nothing for the matter we are treating.
pass_a.217: Relying on the same plural חַיִּים you will have it that the tree of life made for Adam a sure hope of continuing these lives. But it could not have made a sure hope of continuing the sanctity in which you place spiritual life. For God was demanding this continuation from Adam, not promising it to him: who if He had promised it would beyond doubt have made Adam impeccable: for the promise would have been ridiculous—I will bring it about that you persevere in sanctity and justice, provided you do not sin.
pass_a.218: To this triple life you oppose a triple privation or death denounced by God to Adam as a penalty in the words you shall die the death, and you assert that man, just as God had threatened, was dead. But I (with your leave and that of others who think thus with you) cannot transfer those words you shall die the death to spiritual death or the privation of justice and sanctity. Hear, if you please, my reasons, and weigh them: for, unless my mind deceives me, they are not of nothing. First reason. A threat is opposed to a tacit promise, penalty to reward, the death denounced to the life promised. But the life tacitly promised to Adam was not justice or sanctity, unless you wish to confuse the condition of the promise with the thing promised. Therefore the death denounced was not the privation of justice.

213: Chapter IV. Further observations and censures on the same chapter II.

I marked several points, Reverend and most beloved Brother in Christ, in the second chapter of your treatise. Allow me to answer some of them as well. You say things about the breath of life, the tree of life, and the death threatened to Adam. I neither approve those claims, nor see what they do for the thesis you set out to prove in that chapter—but once answered, they can help my case.
214: Starting from the beginning, as they say, you hold that God breathed into man the breath of a threefold life: animal life of the body through the soul's union that keeps it alive; spiritual life of the soul through the Holy Spirit's union that sanctifies it; and blessed life of soul and body through union with God that beats both. Your one proof is that the Hebrew text has the plural חַיִּים, "lives."

That seems to me a very weak prop. The plural is used everywhere for the singular—for that one life you call animal. The examples lie ready: Gen. 3:14; 23:1; 25:7, 17; 27:45; Ps. 17:14; 31:11; Eccles. 2:17; 9:9; and many more. Indeed Gen. 7:15, 22 give even brute animals נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים, the "breath of lives" as you would say—and yet, I think, no life but the animal one, and that without reason.
215: So every interpreter I have seen rendered "life," not "lives." Either they found no mystery in the plural חַיִּים, or they took it to hint at the lives strictly needed for human essence and nature—vegetative, sensitive, and rational—which is Zanchius's and Pareus's view, and not to be scorned.

As the body's formation belonged to making and composing the human being, so did this inspiring of נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים. To that same constitution I gladly also refer sanctity and blessedness, increased when Adam, after he was made, was brought into paradise. Sanctity stood to the soul as health stands to the body.
216: Just as the body did not have a double life with one part seated in health, so I do not think the soul's sanctity adds to the tally of lives Adam had. I see a great gap between Adam's sanctity and ours in Christ. His was natural, created with human nature, and—had it not been lost—would have been passed on by nature's laws, and so was changeable. Ours hangs on the supernatural gift of the Holy Spirit come down from Christ the head into us his members, by which we are regenerated, made alive, and as it were animated and ruled.

Adam's sanctity was a condition of that animal life of his, as you call it—without which the most just and holy God could not have made him, and by which he was well fitted to natural objects. Ours hangs wholly on supernatural revelation, aims wholly at a supernatural object, and lifts us far above Adam's natural, animal, changeable state. So Peter calls it divine nature, and Paul the image of Christ's glory. But this is by the way; it does not touch the point in hand.
217: On the same plural חַיִּים you would have the tree of life give Adam a sure hope of continuing these lives. It could not give a sure hope of continuing the sanctity in which you place spiritual life. God was requiring that continuance from Adam, not promising it to him. Had He promised it, He would beyond doubt have made Adam unable to sin—for the promise would have been absurd: I will make you persevere in sanctity and justice, provided you do not sin.
218: Against this threefold life you set a threefold privation or death, denounced by God to Adam as penalty in the words "you shall die the death," and you claim that man was dead just as God had threatened. For my part (with leave of you and of those who think with you) I cannot shift those words onto spiritual death—the loss of justice and sanctity. Hear my reasons, if you will, and weigh them; unless I am mistaken, they are not empty.

First reason. A threat answers a tacit promise, penalty answers reward, the death denounced answers the life promised. But the life tacitly promised to Adam was not justice or sanctity—unless you confuse the condition of the promise with the thing promised. Therefore the death denounced was not the privation of justice.
